name: THE FRANKIE GOES TO HOLLANDAISE BURGER

recipe.history:
Hollandaise sauce is a classical French emulsion sauce — one of the five mother sauces codified by Auguste Escoffier in the early twentieth century — made from egg yolks, clarified butter, and lemon juice or white wine vinegar. Despite its name suggesting Dutch origins, most food historians believe hollandaise is French in its current form, possibly named for Holland's reputation as a producer of fine butter, or perhaps developed by Huguenot refugees in France. The sauce appears in French culinary texts of the nineteenth century, though similar emulsion sauces using butter and eggs were described earlier. Hollandaise is notoriously temperamental: it is an unstable emulsion that must be made over low, controlled heat — if the eggs get too hot they scramble, too cold and the butter solidifies and the emulsion breaks. Generations of culinary students have been judged on their ability to produce a hollandaise that is smooth, unctuous, pale yellow, and holds its emulsion long enough to be served.

Hollandaise became synonymous in America with Eggs Benedict, the brunch dish attributed to various nineteenth-century New York establishments, and its association with brunch culture made it a slightly formal, occasion-specific sauce in the American kitchen. It began appearing on burgers in the wave of Eggs Benedict-inspired burger creations that swept restaurant menus in the 2010s — a movement that placed a poached or fried egg atop a patty and found that hollandaise was the natural sauce to tie the egg, the beef, and the Canadian bacon together. The combination of hollandaise's rich, lemony butter-fat with the iron-like savoriness of beef is genuinely extraordinary, and the burger world was correct to embrace it.

I burned my first hollandaise. I burned my second hollandaise. I scrambled my third hollandaise. By the fourth attempt I had accepted that hollandaise is a sauce that cannot be rushed, cannot be heated aggressively, and cannot be made while distracted by something else on the stove. It demands full attention and a double boiler or a heatproof bowl set over barely simmering water — not boiling, barely simmering — and a commitment to whisking that will make your forearm ache. When it finally comes together — when the egg yolks thicken and the butter incorporates in a glossy, silky stream and the sauce coats the back of a spoon — the relief and satisfaction are profound. Hollandaise rewards patience and punishes haste. It taught me to slow down in the kitchen.

Hollandaise is a sauce built almost entirely of fat — egg yolk fat and clarified butter fat — and it needs a patty with its own fat contribution to avoid overwhelming the palate. A medium-rare patty at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit has rendered some of its intramuscular fat but retains enough to engage with the hollandaise rather than being drowned by it. The sauce is rich; the patty must be juicy and flavorful enough to hold its own against that richness. An overcooked patty cannot do this — it is dry, it is gray, and the hollandaise sits on top of it like a condiment on cardboard. Medium rare creates the partnership this sauce deserves.
ingredients: 225g unsalted butter, clarified (melt butter, skim foam, pour off clear liquid — discard milky solids)
2 tbsp white wine vinegar (for poaching water)
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let sit 5 minutes. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead on medium 8 minutes. Transfer to oiled bowl, cover, rise 1 to 1.5 hours. Divide into 4 balls, flatten slightly to 4-inch rounds about 1 inch tall. Dust a parchment-lined sheet with semolina. Set rounds on sheet, dust tops with semolina. Cover and proof 45 minutes. Cook in a dry griddle or cast-iron skillet over medium-low heat, covered, 8 minutes per side until cooked through and lightly browned. Cool on rack.

2. Make the clarified butter: Melt 255g unsalted butter in a small saucepan over low heat. Let the foam rise to the top and the milk solids sink. Skim the foam carefully. Slowly pour the clear golden butter into a bowl, leaving the milky white solids behind. You should have approximately 225g clarified butter. Keep warm but not hot.

3. Make the hollandaise: Set a heatproof bowl over a pot of barely simmering water — the bowl must not touch the water. Whisk egg yolks and cold water in the bowl until pale and slightly thickened, about 3 minutes. Remove from heat briefly. Begin drizzling warm clarified butter into the yolks in an extremely slow stream, whisking constantly and vigorously. Return to the double boiler over very low heat periodically as needed. Continue adding butter, whisking, until all butter is incorporated and sauce is thick, glossy, and coats the back of a spoon. Whisk in lemon juice, cayenne, salt, and white pepper. Keep warm over the double boiler with the heat off, whisking occasionally. If the sauce thickens too much, whisk in a few drops of warm water.
4. Cook the Canadian bacon: Sear Canadian bacon slices in a hot skillet over medium-high heat, 2 minutes per side until lightly browned. Set aside and keep warm.

5. Wilt the spinach: Melt butter in the same skillet over medium heat. Add garlic and cook 30 seconds. Add spinach and toss until just wilted, about 90 seconds. Season lightly with salt. Remove from heat.

6. Prepare and cook the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form each into a patty 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Make a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Sear patties 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip and cook 2 to 2.5 minutes more until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). Remove and rest 3 minutes.

7. Poach the eggs: Fill a wide saucepan with 3 inches of water. Add white wine vinegar and bring to a bare simmer — small bubbles, no rolling boil. Crack each egg into a small cup. Create a gentle swirl in the water and slide an egg into the center. Poach 3 minutes for a runny yolk. Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on a paper towel. Repeat for all eggs.
8. Split and toast buns in the skillet fat over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

9. Assemble: Place wilted spinach on the bottom bun half. Set the rested patty on the spinach. Lay a slice of Canadian bacon over the patty. Set a poached egg on top of the bacon. Spoon 2 to 3 tablespoons of hollandaise generously over the poached egg, allowing it to cascade down the sides. Dust with smoked paprika, scatter chives, and add flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun. Serve immediately.
